decision.rationale: The later-sector nominal-aperture period agrees with the published, early SAP and early PDC values. Fit both nominal pixels on the first 70% to forecast their summed counts in electrons/s on the final 30%. Their individual semiamplitudes sum to 24.442 e/s, matching the nominal semiamplitude to the quoted precision and indicating nearly aligned modulation. The second harmonic allows a repeatable departure from a sinusoid. The bright outside aperture shows only 0.428 e/s of modulation at this period. Phase-resolved imaging near predicted maxima and minima could test whether the variable light comes from the nebular candidate or a blended star.

decision.disposition: Fit the rim waveform on the first 70%, calibrate its offset and scale to simultaneous nominal-aperture counts, and forecast the final 30% in electrons/s.
decision.rationale: At the published period, the rim contributes 0.572 electrons/s of semiamplitude from 151 electrons/s of mean light. The brighter core contributes only 0.320 electrons/s, and the nominal aperture shows 0.862 electrons/s. This favors the rim as a tracer. The 11.54-day development span covers nearly four cycles at the published period and less than one at the 12-day maximum. Only the fundamental has a measured amplitude here. A phase-resolved difference image could locate the varying light and test its association with the nebular central star.

Their individual semiamplitudes sum to 24.442 e/s, matching the measured nominal semiamplitude, while the four bright outside pixels together show only 0.428 e/s. decision.rationale: The later-sector nominal aperture recovers the published and early-sector period. Its 24.442 e/s semiamplitude nearly equals the sum of the core and rim semiamplitudes, indicating that both pixels vary in phase. The four bright outside pixels together show only 0.428 e/s. A second harmonic allows unequal minima or a nonsinusoidal peak. The roughly 11.3-hour modulation warrants phase-resolved, higher-resolution imaging to identify the variable star. decision.disposition: Forecast nominal-aperture counts in electrons/s by fitting the rim waveform on the first 70% and calibrating its offset and scale to simultaneous SPOC counts.
decision.rationale: At the published period, the rim shows 0.572 e/s of semiamplitude in 151 e/s of mean flux. The core shows only 0.320 e/s in 413 e/s. The nominal aperture shows 0.862 e/s, consistent with the rim and core variations largely adding in phase. This favors the rim as a predictor, using the single harmonic measured over nearly four development cycles. The 12-day maximum spans less than one cycle in that window. The rim concentration makes blending plausible. A difference image phased at 2.99685 days and registered against catalog stars would test whether the modulation is centered on the nebular candidate or a neighbor.

decision.disposition: Fit one regularized additive waveform directly to nominal-aperture counts.
decision.method: Use elapsed days and fit an intercept plus one sine and cosine pair per listed period. Minimize mean squared error plus lambda_short times the sum of squared coefficients for the first three pairs and lambda_orbit times the sum for the 13.7-day pair. Leave the intercept unpenalized. Choose both penalties from [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100] using only the chronological 70% training prefix. In three validation folds, fit on the first 50%, 60%, and 70% of that prefix, respectively, and score on the next 30% of the prefix in each case. Minimize average fold mean absolute error, breaking ties toward larger lambda_orbit, then larger lambda_short. Refit on the full prefix and evaluate at the final held-out times to obtain electrons/s.
decision.rationale: The two 12-day maxima lie at the search boundary, and the later development span covers less than one such cycle. I use 13.7 days to model possible TESS-orbit background variation. The published 2.99685-day signal has greater absolute semiamplitude in the faint rim than in the bright core (0.572 versus 0.320 electrons/s). The separate 1.175171-day image also peaks outside the early pipeline aperture. Fitting nominal counts lets either modulation contribute in proportion to its measured imprint. For physical follow-up, I would obtain resolved time-series photometry of the nucleus and neighboring stars and compare their phases with the strongest repeatable short-period component before assigning it to the nucleus.
decision.used_material: Supplied period maxima, later development aperture photometry, and the first-sector 1.175171-day harmonic image summary. The 13.7-day term comes from the approximate TESS orbital period.
